already established for the trail / overlay machinery.

Sites converted:

LEXER (highest impact — per-character iteration):
• std/compiler/lexer.ka — main lex_from loop. Per-token append
  was O(N²) per source byte. Now threads (buf, count) through
  tail-recursion via push_tok helper. For a 10KB source: ~2000
  tokens × ~40 bytes/list-copy was ~80MB of allocation churn;
  now ~80KB linear. push_tok is the canonical pattern for
  buffer-extend+set+counter — list_extend_to grows physical
  capacity geometrically (doubling); list_set writes; counter

perennials/3fa0251:
The exported sheet is the picture a client keeps; it cannot be read back.
The full backup restores everything she ever wrote, but a client wants one
garden, not the designer's whole notebook. So a yard now travels on its own:
Share hands over the picture, the plant list, and a .json beside them, and
"Open a yard file" on the Yards tab imports it, so a client's phone becomes
that yard's guide with no account and nothing sent anywhere.

lib/yardFile.ts mirrors backup.ts on every point that matters: a strict
parse that bounces a wrong file rather than half-importing it, the ground
photo carried inside the JSON as a data URL so there is one file and not
two, and the yard written through writeYards so its subscribers re-render.

The one rule it adds, pinned pure in rules.test.ts, is that an import can
never cost her a yard. A file carries the id its yard was saved with, which
can collide with one already on her phone; admitYard gives the newcomer a
fresh id instead of overwriting, because the yard on the phone she is holding
is the one that cannot be replaced by a file from someone else. The ground is
re-keyed under a fresh IndexedDB key on the way in, since the file's key was
minted on another phone and could name a different photo here.
